title: Dr Doofenshmirtz: a trauma-defined yet well-adjusted genius? An Analysis with Informational Computing
text:
In the animated series Phineas and Ferb, the character Dr. Heinz Doofenshmirtz (Doof) is a comic villain with an unusual combination of traits. Defined by his absurdly tragic backstories, Doof is a chaotic mix of a brilliant (albeit ignorant) inventor, an insecure midlifer, and an unexpectly doting father.
This leads me toward a strange conjecture: Dr Doofenshmirtz is a tortured genius who is also well-adjusted.
Naturally, I have no choice but to climb onboard this train of thought and see where it takes me.
In the analysis below, I will explore the validity of this claim by breaking down its exact meaning and structure. Then, I will use the informational programming language Lana to review what evidence from the show supports or contradicts the conjecture, and also what counts as evidence to begin with.
Python is still used for file checks and display.

title: Dr Doofenshmirtz: a trauma-defined yet well-adjusted genius? An Analysis with Informational Computing
text:
1. Semantic Formalization
I have derived 3 claims made in the conjecture about Doof as such:

Genius
Tortured
Well-adjusted

Next, I will formalize each of these claims using this template:
Claim = Semantic Component 1 + … + Semantic Component X
NOTE: These definitions are conceptual models made for the scope of this analysis. It is neither representative of the claims’ total semantical capacity nor an equation meant literally.

Genius = Technical Competence + Originality + Technical Insight
where:

Technical Competence = the ability to apply knowledge/skills to solve problems effectively
Originality = the ability to produce ideas that are meaningfully distinct from what already exists
Technical Insight = the ability to recognize underlying relationships and assumptions within systems that are not immediately apparent


Tortured = Psychological Distress + Perceived Inescapability
where:

Psychological Distress = the intensity of mental or emotional suffering, expressed in words or behavior
Perceived Inescapability = the sense that one’s suffering cannot be resolved or escaped


Well-Adjusted = Emotional Regulation + Psychological Flexibility
where:

Emotional Regulation = the ability to experience and manage emotions without being overwhelmed or controlled by them
Psychological Flexibility = the ability to adapt one’s thoughts, behaviors, and expectations to changing circumstances

3. Evidence Dataset
Episode transcripts are the dataset I will be using for further analysis. They are imported from a public source: https://github.com/captainsidd/phineas-ferb/.
Next, the dataset is reviewed in 3 stages:

Full-inventory AI screening: - gemma4:31b reads each usable transcript and proposed passages relevant to the seven indicators.
AI Passage review: - GPT-6 Astra then reads the selected passages in their original context and checks whether the interpretation fits.
Human review: Read the cited passages and record separate decisions to verify AI-reviewed oberservations. I did not load any separate decisions into the table; the verification passed.

The code below checks the saved files. The next cell sends checked rows to Lana for classification and counts; Python displays the result.

from pathlib import Path

title: Dr Doofenshmirtz: a trauma-defined yet well-adjusted genius? An Analysis with Informational Computing
text:
5. Conclusion
According to the evidence, Doof is good at building things, less so good at inventing new things, and very good at carrying pain.
Yet, he is not stuck there forever: throughout the seasons, he changes his mind, accepts help, and even learns to handles disappointment well.
So “tortured, well-adjusted genius” needs a tune-up; he is a capable, hurting inventor learning to adjust. No Feelings-Fix-inator required.

title: Dr Doofenshmirtz: a trauma-defined yet well-adjusted genius? An Analysis with Informational Computing
text:
Appendix

Scope and Limits
AI can miss scenes, confuse speakers, or misread dreams and alternate stories. Transcripts were not compared to videos.
The 51 observations are selected examples. One passage can support more than one indicator. Repeated clips and time loops can also produce related observations. As a result, the counts do not show how often Doof behaves this way.


Reviewed Evidence
Expand a claim to read its saved observations, interpretation notes, and transcript links.

from html import escape
from IPython.display import HTML

titles = manifest.set_index("episode_id")["title"]
for claim in ledger.index:
    rows = evidence.loc[evidence["claim"].eq(claim)]
    parts = [f"<details><summary><strong>{escape(claim.replace('_', ' ').title())}</strong> — {len(rows)} observations</summary>"]
    for row in rows.itertuples():
        source_link = (
            "https://github.com/captainsidd/phineas-ferb/blob/"
            "b49d21b85f5ae0725a68d414b62f34b069330239/"
            f"{row.source_file.removeprefix('github-transcripts/raw/')}"
            f"#L{row.start_line}-L{row.end_line}"
        )
        parts.append(
            f"<p><strong>{escape(row.evidence_id)} — {escape(titles.loc[row.episode_id])}</strong> · "
            f"{escape(row.indicator.replace('_', ' '))} · {escape(row.polarity)} · "
            f"confidence: {escape(row.confidence)}<br>"
            f"{escape(row.observation)}<br>"
            f"<em>Interpretation:</em> {escape(row.reviewer_note)}<br>"
            f"<a href=\"{escape(source_link, quote=True)}\">Source transcript</a>, "
            f"lines {row.start_line}–{row.end_line}.</p>"
        )
    parts.append("</details>")
    display(HTML("\n".join(parts)))

Genius — 19 observations
E04 — Raging Bully · technical competence · support · confidence: mediumAfter the Slave-inator falls, bystanders report an urge to clean up and start doing so.Interpretation: Consistent with the cleanup function described at lines 94-96; the short transcript does not describe the mechanism or establish general reliability.Source transcript, lines 162–166.
E05 — The Doof Side of the Moon · technical competence · support · confidence: highHis machine fires at the Moon and rotates it; the attached building moves with it.Interpretation: The described mechanical effect succeeds even though his larger plan fails. Confidence concerns the transcript observation, not physical plausibility.Source transcript, lines 159–163.
E06 — The Doof Side of the Moon · originality · ambiguous · confidence: lowHe introduces a device designed to rotate the Moon.Interpretation: An unusual idea is compatible with originality, but this passage provides no comparison with prior inventions. Self-praise does not prove novelty.Source transcript, lines 95–96.
E07 — The Doof Side of the Moon · technical insight · contradict · confidence: highHe expects rotating the Moon to remove the full moon, then notices the failure and recognizes reflected sunlight before proposing rotating the Sun.Interpretation: His stated causal model is mistaken, and the final proposal limits how much credit the correction deserves.Source transcript, lines 175–182.
E09 — The Remains of the Platypus · technical competence · support · confidence: highPerry performs household tasks for Doofenshmirtz and helps expose an intruder.Interpretation: The later flashback at lines 157-160 attributes the changed role to the Butler-inator; the effect is temporary and Perry defeats it.Source transcript, lines 90–98.
E10 — The Remains of the Platypus · technical competence · support · confidence: highAn accidental discharge from the Vaporizer-inator makes Cheesetopia evaporate.Interpretation: Shows a functioning effect within the story, but not successful targeting or control of the Tri-State Area.Source transcript, lines 164–164.
E11 — The Remains of the Platypus · originality · ambiguous · confidence: lowThe Butler-inator combines a tailored outfit with an imposed servant identity and suppressed memory of fighting evil.Interpretation: This is a distinctive combination in the passage; no systematic comparison establishes novelty across the fictional world.Source transcript, lines 157–160.
E12 — The Remains of the Platypus · technical insight · support · confidence: mediumAfter seeing the reminder Perry wrote before the memory change, Doofenshmirtz recognizes how a message to a future self defeats his plan.Interpretation: He recognizes the workaround after the event and admits he did not predict it. This is narrow retrospective insight.Source transcript, lines 157–160.
E14 — Cranius Maximus · technical competence · support · confidence: highHis ray retrieves the ceremonial key; Perry then activates a return setting that releases the collected keys.Interpretation: Supports a functioning collection-and-return mechanism. The device later self-destructs, and the intended universal unlocking goal fails.Source transcript, lines 130–158.
E15 — Cranius Maximus · technical insight · contradict · confidence: highOnly after obtaining the oversized Key to the City does he question whether it is symbolic and too large for ordinary locks.Interpretation: He failed to check a central assumption before building his plan around it.Source transcript, lines 155–158.
E18 — Agent Doof · technical competence · support · confidence: highOnce Norm plugs in the Babe-inator, its beam turns Phineas and Ferb into babies.Interpretation: The transformation works in the narrative; it hits unintended targets and needs someone else to connect power.Source transcript, lines 34–43.
E19 — Agent Doof · technical competence · contradict · confidence: mediumHe interprets the inactive Babe-inator as another failed invention without noticing that it needs to be plugged in.Interpretation: An operational failure weighs against reliable problem solving; it does not erase the working design recorded in E18.Source transcript, lines 34–39.
E23 — Interview With a Platypus · originality · contradict · confidence: mediumHe presents a vehicle that travels on water as his latest invention, calling it BO-AT.Interpretation: The joke describes rediscovering a familiar boat concept. This limits a blanket originality claim; it does not negate his other inventions.Source transcript, lines 78–79.
E34 — Backyard Hodge Podge · technical competence · support · confidence: highHis eye-examination technology is described as being used commercially, with royalties, and his new ray visibly blurs vision.Interpretation: Narrated use and depicted effects support effective application within the fictional world. Commercial details are partly his account.Source transcript, lines 49–54.
E35 — Backyard Hodge Podge · originality · ambiguous · confidence: mediumHe receives royalties for technology used in eye-examination equipment.Interpretation: Adoption gives more context than a self-awarded invention name, but neither royalties nor adoption establishes novelty relative to prior designs.Source transcript, lines 49–54.
E40 — Doof 101 · technical insight · support · confidence: mediumHe obtains Johnny’s hair as a DNA source and plans an antidote while organizing others to find Johnny.Interpretation: The passage links a biological input to a proposed solution within cartoon science. The later reversal supports the plan’s utility, not real-world scientific validity.Source transcript, lines 120–130.
E41 — Doof 101 · technical competence · support · confidence: highThe antidote restores Johnny after Vanessa administers it; Perry helps with the rescue.Interpretation: The substance works, but the delivery is accidental and the rescue is collective. This is not a solo or flawlessly executed success.Source transcript, lines 185–198.
E43 — Last Day of Summer · technical insight · support · confidence: highHe connects repeated events to activation of his Do-Over-inator and identifies the repeating day.Interpretation: A causal inference about the mechanism, supported by the ongoing loop narrative. Recognizing the loop does not mean he foresaw all its consequences.Source transcript, lines 183–194.
E49 — Last Day of Summer · technical competence · support · confidence: highHis activation and Candace’s destruction of the other device coincide with the end of the time loop.Interpretation: The outcome supports a contribution to a working solution. Two simultaneous actions prevent attributing the entire result to him alone.Source transcript, lines 694–710.



Tortured — 13 observations
E01 — Raging Bully · psychological distress · support · confidence: mediumHe describes birthdays as persistently miserable and recalls childhood isolation before announcing a scheme to force people to attend.Interpretation: Reported memories and present motivation support distress. The absurd flashback is narrative evidence, not independently verified biography.Source transcript, lines 85–94.
E02 — Raging Bully · perceived inescapability · ambiguous · confidence: lowHe describes a repeated birthday problem but expects his new device to prevent another lonely birthday.Interpretation: Recurring distress does not establish that he believes relief is impossible; his attempted solution also does not prove that he feels free of suffering.Source transcript, lines 85–94.
E17 — Cranius Maximus · psychological distress · ambiguous · confidence: lowHe links his interest in keys to having been trapped in a cockroach-filled milk can for hours.Interpretation: The event sounds aversive, but this passage does not establish the intensity or persistence of present emotional suffering.Source transcript, lines 45–47.
E22 — Agent Doof · perceived inescapability · contradict · confidence: mediumHe treats repeated failure as a reason to try a different life and seeks employment at the agency.Interpretation: This shows a perceived alternative to his failing role. It is indirect evidence about inescapability of suffering, not proof of psychological well-being.Source transcript, lines 29–36.
E25 — Let's Bounce · psychological distress · support · confidence: mediumAfter the truth ray visibly affects others, a reflected shot makes him disclose that he is secretly very lonely.Interpretation: Within the story the ray makes the admission credible. Loneliness supports distress, but its duration and severity are unspecified.Source transcript, lines 92–100.
E27 — Road to Danville · psychological distress · support · confidence: highStranded and exhausted, he cries and repeatedly calls himself a failure before Perry brings tickets.Interpretation: An explicit episode of suffering and harsh self-judgment. Acute exhaustion contributes; this is not a diagnosis.Source transcript, lines 59–63.
E28 — Road to Danville · perceived inescapability · ambiguous · confidence: mediumHe generalizes that failure has always been his fault, then accepts Perry’s help.Interpretation: Global self-blame suggests entrapment but does not explicitly say relief is impossible. Help changes his immediate response.Source transcript, lines 59–63.
E30 — This Is Your Backstory · perceived inescapability · ambiguous · confidence: mediumPositive memories of Vanessa interrupt his effort to accumulate painful memories and reduce the fictional meter reading.Interpretation: The ordinary framing of this clip show depicts access to positive experience. The meter is a plot device, not a clinical measure, and relief alone does not establish his beliefs about escape.Source transcript, lines 121–141.
E31 — This Is Your Backstory · perceived inescapability · support · confidence: mediumAfter an embarrassing video becomes widely viewed, he says he will never live it down.Interpretation: Explicit language of lasting embarrassment supports a narrow perceived-inescapability reading. It may be comic exaggeration and does not establish permanent entrapment in all suffering.Source transcript, lines 157–160.
E36 — Father's Day · psychological distress · support · confidence: highHe describes Father’s Day as especially difficult and connects it with being forced to serve as a lawn gnome in childhood.Interpretation: The current emotional report matters here; the replayed childhood scene is not treated as a new independent event.Source transcript, lines 46–57.
E37 — Father's Day · perceived inescapability · contradict · confidence: mediumHe believes returning his father’s gnome could let them start again and heal old wounds.Interpretation: This directly expresses a possible route to improvement in a painful relationship. It does not show that the plan will work.Source transcript, lines 46–57.
E38 — Father's Day · psychological distress · support · confidence: highHis father compares the broken gift unfavorably with Roger’s, and Heinz leaves with his voice breaking in tears.Interpretation: Present suffering is depicted, beyond the remembered backstory.Source transcript, lines 131–140.
E45 — Last Day of Summer · perceived inescapability · contradict · confidence: mediumWhen Vanessa challenges his commitment to being evil, he considers that he could become a good person.Interpretation: Her explanation about obligation to backstories is her interpretation. His own willingness to consider another life challenges an unqualified belief that he is trapped.Source transcript, lines 434–451.



Well Adjusted — 19 observations
E03 — Raging Bully · emotional regulation · contradict · confidence: mediumHis response to loneliness includes threatening Perry and planning to compel a crowd to celebrate with him.Interpretation: The explicit link between painful birthdays and coercive action weighs against managing this emotion constructively. Villainy alone would not establish poor regulation.Source transcript, lines 85–98.
E08 — The Doof Side of the Moon · psychological flexibility · ambiguous · confidence: mediumHe initially blames Perry, then changes his explanation when he recognizes that moonlight reflects sunlight.Interpretation: Some updating occurs, but his final proposal keeps the same flawed plan. This is partial flexibility, not a clean recovery.Source transcript, lines 175–182.
E13 — The Remains of the Platypus · psychological flexibility · support · confidence: mediumWhen a musical group unexpectedly crashes into his apartment, he welcomes the group and joins the dancing.Interpretation: A situational change of response is visible; enjoying the interruption does not establish durable adjustment or erase his coercive conduct elsewhere.Source transcript, lines 11–17.
E16 — Cranius Maximus · emotional regulation · support · confidence: mediumAfter Perry destroys the machine, he initially shrugs it off and begins questioning the value of his prize.Interpretation: A brief restrained reaction supports situational regulation. The scene is cut short by lightning; sustained coping is unknown.Source transcript, lines 155–158.
E20 — Agent Doof · psychological flexibility · support · confidence: highAfter repeated perceived failures at evil, he applies to the agency and tries a new role working with Perry.Interpretation: A concrete change of goals and behavior occurs. E21 records its later reversal, so this is not treated as lasting reform.Source transcript, lines 29–36.
E21 — Agent Doof · psychological flexibility · contradict · confidence: mediumAfter being fired, he interprets criticism of the damage he caused as proof that he is good at evil and returns to it.Interpretation: He changes roles again but preserves his destructive goal rather than addressing the feedback. This is a qualified counterexample, not proof of zero adaptability.Source transcript, lines 159–165.
E24 — Phineas and Ferb Summer Belongs to You! · psychological flexibility · support · confidence: mediumHe accepts help from Perry and Monogram to find Vanessa, and father and daughter reconnect in Paris.Interpretation: He cooperates across the usual enemy relationship for his daughter. Her complaint about being put second remains part of the same scene; one reconciliation is not a permanent change.Source transcript, lines 524–548.
E26 — Road to Danville · psychological flexibility · contradict · confidence: mediumHe blames Perry for all his failures and only grudgingly concedes responsibility after his solo attempt fails.Interpretation: Resistance to corrective evidence precedes the change later in this episode.Source transcript, lines 50–57.
E29 — Road to Danville · psychological flexibility · support · confidence: highAfter leaving Perry behind on a bus, he reconsiders, stops the bus, and returns with a jetpack to collect him.Interpretation: The behavior changes after reflection, beyond a verbal promise. His initial abandonment prevents reading the whole sequence as uncomplicated kindness.Source transcript, lines 64–79.
E32 — Fly On the Wall · psychological flexibility · support · confidence: highHe admits a creative block, asks Perry for help, and participates in exercises that lead to a new design.Interpretation: He recognizes a limitation and changes his approach with another person’s help. His goal remains an evil scheme, so flexibility does not imply benevolence.Source transcript, lines 61–74.
E33 — Fly On the Wall · emotional regulation · support · confidence: mediumWhen a falling tire destroys his new machine, he responds with a wry remark about his uncle’s saying.Interpretation: This immediate reaction shows tolerating a setback. It cannot establish regulation in other situations.Source transcript, lines 143–144.
E39 — Father's Day · emotional regulation · support · confidence: mediumAfter the disappointing visit, he accepts Perry’s consolation, appreciates their relationship, and goes home.Interpretation: He acknowledges hurt and seeks connection without retaliating in this passage. Distress and regulation can occur together.Source transcript, lines 131–140.
E42 — Act Your Age · psychological flexibility · support · confidence: mediumIn the future-set episode, he abandons the induced midlife crisis and chooses his familiar life and friends.Interpretation: This is the older Heinz, kept separate from ordinary summer events. He briefly proposes evil and accepts Perry’s correction; change is not flawless.Source transcript, lines 260–265.
E44 — Last Day of Summer · psychological flexibility · contradict · confidence: mediumWhile absorbed in the repeating day, he ignores Vanessa’s attempt to discuss moving out.Interpretation: His initial priorities remain rigid. This is an earlier stage of the same time-loop episode, not a separate independent episode.Source transcript, lines 183–194.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
Programming is a recipe: take inputs, apply rules, produce outputs. Mainstream programming languages generally treat uncertainty as application data rather than a fundamental property of values and computation. Specifically, when information is incomplete, a programmer must manually encode what that uncertainty means and how it should propagate.
What if uncertainty itself became something a program could represent, propagate, reason about, and report?

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
Core Abstraction
The primary conceptual pain point Lana addresses is that most software forces information states into:
KNOW → CONTINUE
DON'T KNOW → ERROR / STOP / GUESS
Lana proposes:
KNOW → CONTINUE
DON'T KNOW  → CONTINUE, PRESERVE UNCERTAINTY
NEED TO ACT → REQUIRE RESOLUTION, THEN CONTINUE
Lana lets programs postpone commitment without postponing computation.
The sections below cover the mathematical specification of how Lana concepts become programmable.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
1. The state
In 1.0, Lana treats uncertainty as a first-class value. Its semantics define STATE, STATE_DIST, and the operations MEASURE, TRANSFORM, and APPEND as primitives.
Importantly, these values describe information about a world. They do not claim to be the world itself.
STATE is a \(2 \times 2\) complex matrix in the set \(\mathcal S\):
\[
\mathcal S = \left\{ \rho \in \mathcal L(\mathbb C^2) \mid \rho = \rho^\dagger,\; \rho \succeq 0,\; \operatorname{Tr}(\rho) = 1 \right\}.
\]
Every state has this form:
\[
\rho = \begin{pmatrix} 1-p & c \\ c^* & p \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The values satisfy \(0 \leq p \leq 1\) and \(|c|^2 \leq p(1-p)\).
The value \(p\) is the probability for outcome \(1\) in the computational basis. The complex value \(c\) is internal state information.
Lana also uses the normalized value \(d\). For \(0 < p < 1\), \(d = c / \sqrt{p(1-p)}\). At \(p = 0\) or \(p = 1\), Lana sets \(d = 0\).
These rules define valid STATE values. Lana treats STATE as an abstract mathematical value. It does not claim that every state is a physical quantum state.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
2. Measuring the state
MEASURE maps a concrete STATE to a probability distribution:
\[
\operatorname{MEASURE}(\rho) = \operatorname{Bernoulli}(p).
\]
The distribution gives outcome \(1\) probability \(p\) and outcome \(0\) probability \(1-p\). The operation reads the state and does not change it.
The computational-basis result depends on \(p\). It does not depend on \(c\) or \(d\). Therefore, two states with the same \(p\) have the same computational-basis measurement distribution.
Lana also defines named binary bases. For the canonical value \(c = \rho_{01}\):
\[
q_{\mathrm{computational}}(\rho)=p,\qquad q_x(\rho)=\frac12-\operatorname{Re}(c),\qquad q_y(\rho)=\frac12+\operatorname{Im}(c).
\]
Named-basis measurement remains read-only. It does not collapse or replace the input state.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
3. Transforming the state
A valid transform is a deterministic, Borel-measurable function:
\[
\Phi : \mathcal S \rightarrow \mathcal S.
\]
The transform must return a valid STATE for every input in its declared domain. Its output must satisfy \(0 \leq p' \leq 1\) and \(|c'|^2 \leq p'(1-p')\).
Valid transforms compose. Composition is associative, and the identity transform exists.
A transform does not need an inverse. Therefore, valid transforms form a monoid, not necessarily a group.
Lana 1.0 registers INVERT and NEUTRALIZE as operands for transformation. INVERT changes \((p,d)\) to \((1-p,\overline d)\). NEUTRALIZE changes \((p,d)\) to \((p,0)\). Both transforms preserve the state rules.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
4. Appending states
APPEND(A, B) accepts two concrete STATE values and returns a STATE_DIST. For this operation, Lana models the two represented events as independent. The operation does not state that all events are independent.
If the input probabilities are \(p_A\) and \(p_B\), the output probability is:
\[
p_C = 1-(1-p_A)(1-p_B).
\]
The output distribution contains valid states with this value of \(p_C\). Lana computes the distribution of the internal value \(d_C\) from \(d_A\) and \(d_B\).
For \(0 < p_C < 1\), define:
\[
m_C=\frac{d_A+d_B}{2},\qquad \sigma_C=\frac{|d_A-d_B|}{2}.
\]
If \(\sigma_C > 0\), \(d_C\) has a truncated circular complex-normal distribution on the unit disk. If \(\sigma_C = 0\), \(d_C\) has a Dirac distribution at \(m_C\). If \(p_C\) is \(0\) or \(1\), \(d_C\) has a Dirac distribution at \(0\).
The observable probability is bounded and associative. The internal distribution is evaluated as a binary tree. Lana 1.0 gives no associativity guarantee for that internal distribution.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
5. Composition semantics
Lana evaluates nested operations in their written order. In:
APPEND(APPEND(A, B), C)
the runtime evaluates APPEND(A, B) first. It then applies APPEND to that result and C by the declared lifted rules. It does not rewrite the expression with a different grouping.
Lana embeds a concrete state \(\rho\) in a distribution as the Dirac distribution \(\delta_\rho\). This embedding lets lifted operations use a concrete state as a degenerate STATE_DIST.
For a valid transform \(\Phi\) and a distribution \(\mu\), the lifted transform is the pushforward \(\Phi_*\mu\). It applies the deterministic transform to each state in the distribution.
The lifted APPEND applies the ordinary APPEND rule to states from the input distributions. The output is the resulting distribution over states.
MEASURE of a STATE_DIST returns a probability distribution. Its outcome-1 probability is the exact expectation of the state probability:
\[
P(X=1)=\int_{\mathcal S}p(\rho)\,d\mu(\rho).
\]
Sampling is separate from these exact operations. SAMPLE_STATE_DIST returns one concrete state and does not mutate the source distribution.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
6. Boundary conditions and failure handling
The runtime rejects a STATE when \(p\) is outside \([0,1]\) or \(|c|^2 > p(1-p)\). It does not reinterpret invalid input as another state.
At \(p=0\) or \(p=1\), the state rule requires \(c=0\). Lana sets \(d=0\) at both boundaries.
The runtime handles APPEND degeneracy explicitly. It uses the Dirac distribution at \(d_C=0\) when \(p_C\) is \(0\) or \(1\). It uses the Dirac distribution at \(d_C=m_C\) when \(0 < p_C < 1\) and \(\sigma_C=0\).
A transform is invalid for an input when its output does not satisfy the STATE invariant. The runtime rejects that result.
Each operation has a declared domain. Unsupported type combinations return an error. Lana does not perform an implicit conversion unless the semantics define it.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
text:
7. Implementation obligations
The runtime must retain enough information to reconstruct \(p\) and \(c\). If it stores \(d\), it must preserve the full complex value and reconstruct \(c=d\sqrt{p(1-p)}\).
STATE_DIST is a finite lazy expression over STATE values. It is not an enumeration of every possible state. A chain can remain a tree until measurement or sampling needs a result.
The C runtime uses a tolerance of \(\varepsilon=10^{-12}\) for accepted floating-point boundary error. This tolerance supports numerical representation. It does not expand the mathematical state domain.
Sampling uses a seeded pseudo-random source. The runtime and VM documents define stream ownership and algorithm details.

title: Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?
section: Conclusion, or why this article answers the title question
text:
Conclusion, or why this article answers the title question
Uncertainty is programmable, provided its representation is precise, operations well-defined, and failures caught rather than silently hidden.
Other languages make the programmer build uncertainity semantics, whereas Lana 1.0 treats uncertainty as data — a first-class value (STATE, STATE_DIST) with well-defined operations (MEASURE, TRANSFORM, APPEND, SAMPLE, CONDITION, etc.).
The key insight is that when uncertainty is treated as data, the program becomes a reasoning machine rather than a deterministic value transformer. Everything that can be composed follows from well-defined mathematical rules.

title: Why should you accumulate BTC?
text:
The world we live in is becoming increasingly abstract; along with the tangible, physical world that all living creatures inhabit, there exists a digital world consisting of networks and systems with mind-boggling layers of connectivity to power our growing needs.
Today, the demands of that digital world have become large enough to demand its own economy; as global commerce becomes increasingly digital, we have outgrown the limitations of centralized financial systems and geography. A new question emerged: how can we support the scale and speed demands of modern commerce without breaking physical limitations or the social contract of trust?
Enter, cryptocurrency. We now have an elegant solution for a number of bottlenecks that traditional financial infrastructure can struggle with: trusted accounting, 24/7 settlement, transparent auditability, double spending. We can even program our own money now rather than relying on minted coins and notes, furthering the abstraction of money as a mode of transaction. This logic is particularly true for Bitcoin, which has earned a public reputation as “digital gold”.
Bitcoin has become an investable asset for a simple reason: a growing number of people and institutions want exposure to a scarce, globally transferable digital asset. Its fixed issuance schedule and expanding network further support an investment thesis. However, that thesis comes with an important warning. Bitcoin has already experienced enormous drawdowns, and its future adoption and price remain uncertain. From a portfolio perspective, the question is therefore not only why own BTC, but also how to build a position without relying on a perfect entry point.

title: Why should you accumulate BTC?
text:
Methodology
This study asks two questions.

How did Bitcoin perform compared to the S&P 500 over the same period using equal periodic dollar-cost averaging?
Does the choice of accumulation engine — DCA, value averaging, or buy-the-dip — change the outcome when each engine is applied to both assets?

The backtest runs the same dollar contribution targets on BTC-USD and SPY. It compares ending value, cash required, capital efficiency, and drawdown. BTC trades every day, while SPY contributes on its valid market-trading days. When a calendar purchase date is not a trading day for SPY, the purchase occurs on the first available observation on or after that date.
This is a historical experiment, not a forecast or personal investment advice. The baseline excludes fees, spreads, slippage, and taxes. Every strategy is long-only: it can buy the tested asset, but never sells it.
The analysis uses BTC-USD daily candles from Coinbase and adjusted SPY daily prices from Yahoo Finance between July 3, 2021 and July 2, 2026.

from datetime import date, timedelta
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

START_DATE = date(2021, 7, 3)

# Downloads Coinbase daily candles in small public-API windows.
def fetch_coinbase_daily_candles(start_date, end_date):
    rows = []
    window_start = start_date
    while window_start <= end_date:
        window_end = min(window_start + timedelta(days=299), end_date)
        query = urlencode({"granularity":86400, "start":f"{window_start}T00:00:00Z", "end":f"{window_end + timedelta(days=1)}T00:00:00Z"})
        request = Request(f"https://api.exchange.coinbase.com/products/BTC-USD/candles?{query}", headers={"User-Agent":"data-articles-btc-study/1.0"})
        with urlopen(request, timeout=30) as response:
            rows.extend(json.loads(response.read().decode("utf-8")))
        window_start = window_end + timedelta(days=1)
        time.sleep(0.2)
    candles = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["timestamp","low","high","open","close","volume"])
    candles["date"] = pd.to_datetime(candles["timestamp"], unit="s", utc=True).dt.tz_localize(None).dt.normalize()
    return candles[["date","open","high","low","close","volume"]].drop_duplicates("date").sort_values("date").reset_index(drop=True)

# Loads the BTC cache or creates it from Coinbase.
def load_btc_data(path):
    if path.exists():
        data = pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date"])
        print(f"Loaded cached BTC data: {path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}")
    else:
        print("No BTC cache found; downloading Coinbase candles...")
        data = fetch_coinbase_daily_candles(START_DATE, END_DATE)
        data.to_csv(path, index=False)
    data["date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["date"]).dt.normalize()
    data["close"] = pd.to_numeric(data["close"], errors="coerce")
    return data[data["date"].between(pd.Timestamp(START_DATE), pd.Timestamp(END_DATE))].dropna(subset=["close"]).sort_values("date").drop_duplicates("date").reset_index(drop=True)

# Downloads and caches adjusted SPY prices from Yahoo Finance.
def load_spy_data(path):
    if path.exists():
        data = pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date"])
        print(f"Loaded cached SPY data: {path.relative_to(REPO_ROOT)}")
    else:
        print("No SPY cache found; downloading adjusted Yahoo Finance prices...")
        downloaded = yf.download("SPY", start=str(START_DATE), end=str(END_DATE + timedelta(days=1)), auto_adjust=True, progress=False)
        if downloaded.empty:
            raise RuntimeError("Yahoo Finance returned no SPY data.")

            close = close.iloc[:, 0]
        data = close.rename("close").rename_axis("date").reset_index()

        data.to_csv(path, index=False)
    data["date"] = pd.to_datetime(data["date"]).dt.normalize()
    data["close"] = pd.to_numeric(data["close"], errors="coerce")

asset_data = {"BTC": load_btc_data(BTC_PATH), "SPY": load_spy_data(SPY_PATH)}
for asset, data in asset_data.items():
    print(f"{asset}: {len(data):,} rows, {data['date'].min().date()} through {data['date'].max().date()}, duplicates={data['date'].duplicated().sum()}")

Now that the data is loaded, let’s define the accumulation engines for each portfolio prior to the backtest.

title: Why should you accumulate BTC?
text:
Accumulation Engines

Dollar-cost averaging (DCA): buy the same dollar amount on a regular schedule.
Value averaging: set a target path for the portfolio and buy more when the portfolio falls behind that path; buy less or nothing when it is ahead.
Buy-the-dip: keep the dollar amount fixed, but buy only after the asset falls by a chosen percentage over a chosen period.


Configurations

DCA: buy $100 at month-end, regardless of the price. This means partial buys for BTC and SPY are enabled.
Value averaging: a target path that grows by $100 every month-end.
Buy-the-dip: buy $100 at month-end after a 10% one-month decline.

The same dollar targets are applied to both BTC and SPY. For SPY, purchases execute on the first available trading day on or after the calendar target.

# Maps calendar targets to the first valid observation for an asset.
def execution_dates(asset_dates, cadence):
    dates = pd.Series(pd.to_datetime(asset_dates).drop_duplicates().sort_values())
    if cadence == "daily":
        targets = pd.date_range(dates.iloc[0], dates.iloc[-1], freq="D")
    elif cadence == "weekly":
        targets = pd.date_range(dates.iloc[0], dates.iloc[-1], freq="7D")
    else:
        targets = pd.date_range(dates.iloc[0] + pd.offsets.MonthEnd(0), dates.iloc[-1], freq="ME")
    return pd.Index(dates.iloc[np.searchsorted(dates.values, targets.values, side="left")].drop_duplicates())

# Builds a fixed-dollar DCA schedule using calendar targets.
def dca_purchases(data, amount, cadence):
    return {pd.Timestamp(day): float(amount) for day in execution_dates(data["date"], cadence)}

# Builds purchases that keep the portfolio on a planned value path.
def value_average_purchases(data, amount, cadence):
    dates = execution_dates(data["date"], cadence)
    prices = data.set_index("date")["close"]
    purchases, held, target = {}, 0.0, 0.0
    for day in dates:
        target += amount
        price = prices.loc[day]
        purchase = max(0.0, target - held * price)
        if purchase > 0:
            purchases[day] = purchase
            held += purchase / price
    return purchases

# Buys at month-end only when the asset has fallen by a specified trailing amount.
def dip_purchases(data, amount, lookback, threshold, cadence="monthly"):
    prices = data.set_index("date")["close"]
    signal_dates = execution_dates(data["date"], cadence)
    trailing_returns = prices / prices.shift(lookback) - 1
    signal_dates = [day for day in signal_dates if trailing_returns.get(day, np.nan) <= threshold]
    return {pd.Timestamp(day): float(amount) for day in signal_dates}

# Creates a complete portfolio history from an asset and purchase ledger.
def build_portfolio(data, purchases, asset, engine):
    history = data[["date","close"]].copy()
    history["purchase"] = history["date"].map(purchases).fillna(0.0)
    history["units_bought"] = history["purchase"] / history["close"]
    history["cash_contributed"] = history["purchase"].cumsum()
    history["units_held"] = history["units_bought"].cumsum()
    history["portfolio_value"] = history["units_held"] * history["close"]
    history["running_peak"] = history["portfolio_value"].cummax()
    history["drawdown"] = history["portfolio_value"] / history["running_peak"] - 1
    history["asset"], history["engine"] = asset, engine
    return history

engine_specs = {
    "DCA $100 month-end": ("dca", 100, "monthly"),
    "Value avg $100 month-end": ("value", 100, "monthly"),
    "Buy dip $100 after -10% month": ("dip", 100, "monthly"),
}

portfolios = {}
for asset, data in asset_data.items():
    for engine, (kind, amount, cadence) in engine_specs.items():
        if kind == "dca": purchases = dca_purchases(data, amount, cadence)
        elif kind == "value": purchases = value_average_purchases(data, amount, cadence)
        else:
            lookback = {"BTC":30, "SPY":21}[asset]
            purchases = dip_purchases(data, amount, lookback, -0.10, cadence)
        portfolios[(asset, engine)] = build_portfolio(data, purchases, asset, engine)

print(f"Built {len(portfolios)} asset-engine histories.")

Built 6 asset-engine histories.


Now, let’s perform the backtest via calculating money-weighted annual return. This metric measures an investor’s actual annualized experience while accounting for where and how much money each accumulation strategy contributed.
For results, the same metrics are used for every asset-engine pair so that a higher ending value is not confused with better capital efficiency.

# Calculates money-weighted annual return from dated cash flows.
def calculate_irr(history):
    invested = history[history["purchase"] > 0]
    if invested.empty: return np.nan
    flows = [-x for x in invested["purchase"]] + [float(history.iloc[-1]["portfolio_value"])]
    dates = list(invested["date"]) + [history.iloc[-1]["date"]]
    years = np.array([(day - dates[0]).days / 365.25 for day in dates])
    def npv(rate): return sum(flow / (1 + rate) ** year for flow, year in zip(flows, years))
    low, high = -0.9999, 100.0
    if npv(low) * npv(high) > 0: return np.nan
    for _ in range(150):
        mid = (low + high) / 2
        if npv(low) * npv(mid) <= 0: high = mid
        else: low = mid
    return (low + high) / 2

# Summarizes every asset-engine combination on the same metrics.
def summarize(history):
    invested = history["purchase"].sum()
    ending = history.iloc[-1]["portfolio_value"]
    return {"Asset":history.iloc[0]["asset"], "Engine":history.iloc[0]["engine"], "Buys":int((history["purchase"] > 0).sum()), "Total Invested":invested, "Ending Value":ending, "Profit":ending-invested, "Return on Cash":ending/invested-1 if invested else np.nan, "IRR":calculate_irr(history), "Max Drawdown":history["drawdown"].min(), "Days Below Cash":(history["portfolio_value"] < history["cash_contributed"]).mean()}

results = pd.DataFrame([summarize(history) for history in portfolios.values()])
display(results.sort_values(["Engine","Asset"]).reset_index(drop=True).style.format({"Total Invested":"${:,.0f}","Ending Value":"${:,.0f}","Profit":"${:,.0f}","Return on Cash":"{:.1%}","IRR":"{:.1%}","Max Drawdown":"{:.1%}","Days Below Cash":"{:.1%}"}))

title: Why should you accumulate BTC?
text:
Results
The fairest comparison is the shared $100 month-end DCA baseline: over this study window, SPY finished with the higher portfolio value and a much smaller drawdown than BTC. The DCA rows answer the direct BTC-versus-SPY accumulation question.
The value averaging results look more interesting: BTC looked more attractive because it produced a higher return on the cash actually invested, but it also deployed a different amount of capital and experienced a deeper drawdown.
The most direct conclusion is that SPY was the more consistent accumulation asset in this sample, while BTC offered greater upside potential only through a more volatile and capital-sensitive path.

title: Why should you accumulate BTC?
text:
Conclusion
This experiment answers two questions that are often mixed together: whether BTC outperformed SPY as an accumulation asset, and whether a particular accumulation engine improved the outcome. Equal periodic DCA provides the clean baseline, whereas value averaging and buy-the-dip portfolios showcase how adaptive rules change cash deployment, ending value, and drawdown.
Over the backtest’s five-year span, SPY was the stronger and more consistent accumulation asset under the fairest comparison: investing the same $100 at month-end produced a higher ending value, higher money-weighted return, and much smaller drawdown than BTC. However, BTC became more attractive under value averaging, which produced a higher return on contributed cash, even though that came with deeper drawdowns and different capital deployment.
To answer the original question: accumulate BTC if you believe bigger risk begets bigger rewards in the financial markets.

title: Why should you accumulate BTC?
text:
Limitations

BTC trades continuously while SPY trades only on exchange days; the notebook uses each asset’s first valid observation on or after a calendar target.
SPY uses adjusted Yahoo Finance prices; BTC uses Coinbase closes. These are comparable daily proxies, not identical execution venues.
Fees, spreads, slippage, and taxes are excluded.
The study covers one historical window and does not establish future performance.
Value averaging has no maximum purchase cap in this baseline.
The SPY buy-the-dip rule did not trigger during this sample, so its zero-investment result is not a meaningful performance comparison.
Value averaging does not contribute the same total cash as DCA; its return-on-cash comparison reflects that different capital deployment.
The study is educational and not personalized financial advice.

title: What makes a basketball team win?
text:
The first time I watched Shai Gilgeous-Alexander play on TV, I was treated to the statistic that it was his 20th consecutive game in which he had scored 20+ points (against the Suns on November 28, 2025). His stellar season performance did not taper off into playoffs; he posted eye-popping averages of 27.6 points and 7.9 assists per game.
Yet, Oklahoma City failed to repeat as champions, thanks in part to a San Antonio defense spearheaded by Victor Wembanyama.
That got me wondering:
Let’s investigate.

title: What makes a basketball team win?
text:
Methodology
What I’m solving for can be described in 2 ways:

If we know how often a team shoots, rebounds, passes, steals, blocks shots, and turns the ball over, can we estimate how likely the team is to win?
win probability per match (%) = (a * box_score_metric_1) + (b * box_score_metric_2) + ... + intercept

To conduct this experiment, I am using a type of regression model called Elastic Net.
I chose this regression in particular for two reasons:

Many basketball statistics are related to one another.

Teams that score more points (PTS) often record more assists (AST).
Teams that shoot efficiently (FG_PCT) tend to win more games (WIN_PCT).

I don’t know beforehand which statistics matter most.

Some statistics may provide unique information.
Others may simply tell us the same story in a different way.


Elastic Net helps solve this problem by automatically identifying the most useful metrics while reducing the influence of redundant ones.

title: What makes a basketball team win?
text:
Running the Experiment
Let’s jump into the code.
I’m using 2 datasets:

2021-2026 regular season. 5 seasons, 30 teams, and 82 games/season/team - a healthy sample size for this regression.
2021-2026 playoffs.


from pathlib import Path
import time

import pandas as pd
from nba_api.stats.endpoints import leaguegamelog
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNetCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

'''
The notebook keeps raw game logs locally, then builds the team-season table from those games.
'''

# Seasons included in the analysis.
seasons = ["2021-22", "2022-23", "2023-24", "2024-25", "2025-26"]

# Local CSV files keep NBA.com downloads from running every time.
REPO_ROOT = Path.cwd().parent if Path.cwd().name == "website" else Path.cwd()
DATA_DIR = REPO_ROOT / "data/nba"
DATA_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

files = {
    "regular_season": DATA_DIR / "nba_team_games_regular_season.csv",
    "playoffs": DATA_DIR / "nba_team_games_playoffs.csv",
}

Let’s fetch the data from the nba_api library and print column headers for the regular season to see what we’re working with.

# Gets one row per team-game from NBA.com for each season.
def fetch_games(season_type):
    all_seasons = []

    for season in seasons:
        print(f"Fetching {season} {season_type} games...")

        games = leaguegamelog.LeagueGameLog(
            player_or_team_abbreviation="T",
            season=season,
            season_type_all_star=season_type,
            timeout=60,
        ).get_data_frames()[0]

        games["SEASON"] = season
        games["SEASON_TYPE"] = season_type
        all_seasons.append(games)
        time.sleep(1)

    return pd.concat(all_seasons, ignore_index=True)


# Uses the local CSV if it exists; otherwise fetches the data once and saves it.
def load_or_fetch(path, fetch_fn):
    if path.exists():
        print(f"Loading local file: {path}")
        return pd.read_csv(path)

    data = fetch_fn()
    data.to_csv(path, index=False)
    return data


# Turns one row per team-game into one row per team-season.
def summarize_team_seasons(games):
    games = games.copy()

    # A team's blocks against are the opponent's blocks in the same game.
    opponent_totals = games.groupby("GAME_ID")[["BLK", "PF"]].transform("sum")
    games["BLKA"] = opponent_totals["BLK"] - games["BLK"]
    games["PFD"] = opponent_totals["PF"] - games["PF"]

    # Wins come directly from the game result column.
    games["WIN"] = games["WL"].eq("W").astype(int)

    team_columns = ["SEASON", "SEASON_TYPE", "TEAM_ID", "TEAM_ABBREVIATION", "TEAM_NAME"]
    stats_to_sum = [
        "MIN", "FGM", "FGA", "FG3M", "FG3A", "FTM", "FTA",
        "OREB", "DREB", "REB", "AST", "STL", "BLK", "BLKA",
        "TOV", "PF", "PFD", "PTS", "PLUS_MINUS",
    ]

    record = games.groupby(team_columns, as_index=False).agg(
        GP=("GAME_ID", "count"),
        W=("WIN", "sum"),
    )
    totals = games.groupby(team_columns, as_index=False)[stats_to_sum].sum()
    summary = record.merge(totals, on=team_columns)

    # Rebuild the summary stats from the game rows.
    summary["L"] = summary["GP"] - summary["W"]
    summary["W_PCT"] = summary["W"] / summary["GP"]
    summary["FG_PCT"] = summary["FGM"] / summary["FGA"]
    summary["FG3_PCT"] = summary["FG3M"] / summary["FG3A"]
    summary["FT_PCT"] = summary["FTM"] / summary["FTA"]

    per_game_cols = [
    "FGA", "FG3A", "REB", "AST", "STL", "BLK", "BLKA",
    "TOV", "PF", "PFD", "PTS", "PLUS_MINUS",
    "OREB", "DREB", "FGM", "FG3M", "FTM", "FTA",
]

    for col in per_game_cols:
        summary[f"{col}_PG"] = summary[col] / summary["GP"]

    return summary

df_regular_season = load_or_fetch(
    files["regular_season"],
    lambda: fetch_games("Regular Season"),
)

df_playoffs = load_or_fetch(
    files["playoffs"],
    lambda: fetch_games("Playoffs"),
)

print("Regular-season team-game rows:", len(df_regular_season))
print("Playoff team-game rows:", len(df_playoffs))
df_model_source = summarize_team_seasons(df_regular_season)
df_playoffs_model_source = summarize_team_seasons(df_playoffs)
print("Regular-season team-season cols:\n", df_model_source.columns)

    "FGA_PG", "FG3A_PG", "FTA_PG", "OREB_PG", "DREB_PG", "AST_PG",

Now, we have defined that the regression will use per-game shooting volume, rebounding, passing, defensive activity, turnovers, and shooting efficiency to estimate team win percentage.
Next, we will build the model.

X = df_model.drop(columns=["W_PCT"])

text:
Findings
Across both regular season data and playoffs data, the biggest finding is that shooting efficiency matters most. FG_PCT and FG3_PCT are the strongest factors in determining win rate.
The per-game stats also make a lot of sense:

More steals -> higher expected win percentage.
More turnovers -> lower expected win percentage.
More offensive/defensive rebounds -> higher expected win percentage.

The main difference is that shooting efficiency matters much more in the regular-season model.

title: Quantifying Forecast Accuracy: The Brier Score
text:
In quantitative research, just as in life, we rarely deal with certainties. Instead, we deal with probabilities. But how do you measure if a probabilistic forecast is actually “good”?
Introducing: the Brier Score.
Unlike simple accuracy (which only asks if you were right or wrong), the Brier Score asks: How confident were you in the right answer?

title: Quantifying Forecast Accuracy: The Brier Score
text:
The Mathematics of Certainty
The Brier Score is essentially the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of a probability forecast:
\[\text{BS} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{t=1}^{N} (f_t - o_t)^2\]

\(f_t\): The forecast probability (e.g., \(0.7\) for a 70% chance of a price increase).
\(o_t\): The actual outcome (\(1\) if the price increased, \(0\) if it didn’t).


Interpreting the Result

0.0: Perfect forecast (you assigned 100% probability to everything that happened).
0.25: The “Naive” score (assigning 50% to everything—essentially a coin flip).
1.0: Worst possible forecast (you were 100% sure the opposite would happen).

title: Quantifying Forecast Accuracy: The Brier Score
text:
Example
Let’s consider a practical model for the Brier Score - Bitcoin (BTC) prices.
First, let’s retrieve one year’s worth of BTC data. Then, for each day, we will create a label for whether the next day’s closing price is higher than today’s.
This is a teaching example: we will score an illustrative momentum rule, not test an investment strategy.

import yfinance as yf
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Download one year of daily BTC closes.
btc = yf.download('BTC-USD', period='1y', interval='1d', progress=False)
close = btc['Close']
if isinstance(close, pd.DataFrame):
    close = close.iloc[:, 0]

df = pd.DataFrame({'close': close})
# Outcome: 1 when tomorrow closes above today; the final day has no known outcome.
df['outcome'] = (df['close'].shift(-1) > df['close']).astype(float)
df.loc[df.index[-1], 'outcome'] = np.nan

# Input: whether today's close rose from yesterday's close.
df['today_up'] = (df['close'] > df['close'].shift(1)).astype(float)
df.loc[df.index[0], 'today_up'] = np.nan
df = df.dropna(subset=['outcome', 'today_up']).copy()
assert df['outcome'].isin([0.0, 1.0]).all()
assert df['today_up'].isin([0.0, 1.0]).all()
print(f"BTC data through {df.index.max().date()}; scored days: {len(df):,}")

BTC data through 2026-09-03; scored days: 364

title: Quantifying Forecast Accuracy: The Brier Score
text:
Scenario 1: The Naive Baseline
If we have no view on tomorrow’s direction, we can assign a constant 50% probability of an increase.

df['naive_prob'] = 0.5
naive_bs = np.mean((df['naive_prob'] - df['outcome'])**2)
print(f"Naive Brier Score: {naive_bs:.4f}")

Naive Brier Score: 0.2500

title: Quantifying Forecast Accuracy: The Brier Score
text:
Scenario 2: A Simple Momentum Rule
Let’s construct an illustrative momentum rule. These 60% and 40% probabilities are chosen for demonstration, not estimated from the data.

If BTC rose today, forecast a 60% chance that it rises tomorrow.
If BTC fell today, forecast a 40% chance that it rises tomorrow.


df['momentum_prob'] = np.where(df['today_up'] == 1, 0.6, 0.4)
momentum_bs = np.mean((df['momentum_prob'] - df['outcome'])**2)
print(f"Momentum Brier Score: {momentum_bs:.4f}")

Momentum Brier Score: 0.2556



results = pd.DataFrame({
    'Forecast': ['Neutral 50%', 'Illustrative momentum'],
    'Brier score': [naive_bs, momentum_bs],
})
print(results.to_string(index=False, formatters={'Brier score': '{:.4f}'.format}))

             Forecast Brier score
          Neutral 50%      0.2500
Illustrative momentum      0.2556

title: Quantifying Forecast Accuracy: The Brier Score
text:
Takeaway
The Brier score gives us a better way to judge probability forecasts than simply counting correct guesses. In this one-year BTC example, the illustrative momentum rule scored slightly worse than a neutral 50% forecast, so its confidence did not improve the forecast on this sample.
That does not mean momentum can never matter in markets; it means that a rule should earn our confidence through measured results, not intuition alone.

title: Can Lana Learn From Real Data?
text:
In Can Uncertainty Be Programmable?, Lana reasoned about values that I explicitly handed the program.
An obvious, consequential next question follows: can Lana learn those values from data instead?
To find out, I gave Lana a small machine-learning job: train a decision tree. Then I checked every answer against scikit-learn, Python’s standard library for this kind of model.

title: Can Lana Learn From Real Data?
text:
Lana’s ML Capabilities
A decision tree learns a chain of yes/no questions from examples. To make a prediction, it follows those questions down to an answer. Every prediction has a path you can read; that path is why this model was the right first test for Lana.
This is the whole program for one comparison (the file path is shortened):
import "std/trees" as trees
let data = resolve(result_value(json_parse(read_text("pima-42.json"))))
let result = trees.fit(data.task, data.train, data.holdout, {family: "tree", max_depth: 4, min_leaf: 2, ensemble_size: 1, seed: 42})
print(json_stringify(result.validation_report))
It loads the data, trains the tree, scores it on held-out rows and prints a report.

title: Can Lana Learn From Real Data?
text:
The Data
I used two public datasets:

Banknote Authentication: 1,372 rows with 4 features measured from banknote images. The task is to label each note genuine or forged.
Pima diabetes: 768 rows with 8 health measurements, such as glucose and BMI. The task is to predict the yes/no diabetes label.

For each dataset, I made two train/test splits. Each split used about 80% of the rows to train and 20% to test. Rows with identical feature values were always kept on the same side, so no test row was also a training row.
I tried two tree depths: depth 4, which allows a shorter chain of questions, and depth 6, which allows more detailed rules. Both got the same rows, feature order, depth and minimum leaf size.
Two datasets × two splits × two depths gives eight comparisons. The two splits share some rows, so the 1,712 predictions are counted per comparison, not as unique rows.

title: Can Lana Learn From Real Data?
text:
Why This Matters
Lana now does more than calculate with values you give it. It takes real examples, learns a model and predicts on data it hasn’t seen, and the predictions match scikit-learn at the tested scale.
The bigger idea is what happens next. A decision tree doesn’t just give an answer; it gives the chain of questions that led there. Lana’s tree interface can expose that chain. That fits naturally with Lana’s information model, where a learned prediction would carry its evidence and uncertainty forward.
This experiment establishes the learning piece. Wiring it into the uncertainty model is the next piece.

def first_measured(runs, **match):
    out = {}
    for r in runs:
        if r["phase"] == "measured" and all(r[k] == v for k, v in match.items()):
            out.setdefault(r["implementation"], r)
    return out

diffs = []
for r in perf:
    pair = first_measured(perf_runs, dataset=r["dataset"], split=r["seed"], depth=r["depth"])
    label = f'{"Banknote" if r["dataset"] == "banknote" else "Diabetes"} split {r["seed"]}, depth {r["depth"]}'
    sk = {p["id"]: p for p in pair["sklearn"]["predictions"]}
    for p in pair["lana"]["predictions"]:
        if p["prediction"] != sk[p["id"]]["prediction"]:
            diffs.append((label, p["id"], p["prediction"], sk[p["id"]]["prediction"], p["target"]))
for n in sorted({r["rows"] for r in rows}):
